main.title: Animal Crossing: New Leaf
main.subtitle: A new arrival becomes the town mayor
main.summary: Animal Crossing: New Leaf is a social simulation game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 3DS.

cards.heading: A new arrival becomes the town mayor
cards.text:
Animal Crossing: New Leaf is a social simulation game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 3DS. The game was first released in 2012 in Japan and later worldwide in 2013, it is the fourth main game in the Animal Crossing series. The player controls a human character who takes on the role of mayor in a town populated with anthropomorphic animals.

The player has the ability to do activities such as bug catching, fishing, and befriending villagers. While retaining gameplay from older titles, Animal Crossing: New Leaf marks a change in the series, as the player becomes the mayor of the town, granting additional abilities such as to enact ordinances and start public works projects. With the help of the townsfolk and a secretary named Isabelle, it is now the player's job to make the town a better place to live.

cards.heading: Everyday activities follow the real-world clock
cards.text: As in the previous installments of the Animal Crossing series, players take control of a villager who is moving into a new town. Upon arrival, the player is mistaken for the new town mayor and is given that position instead of being a standard resident. Like the previous games in the series, the game enables the player to explore their town, talk with other residents, and participate in various activities such as fishing and bug catching. Doing various activities or selling various items earns the player Bells, the game's currency, which they can use to purchase various items such as furniture or clothes, or pay loans used to renovate their house. The game is played in real-time, utilizing the Nintendo 3DS system's internal clock, with aspects such as shop opening times, species of wildlife and special events varying depending on the time of day and season.

cards.heading: Public projects and ordinances reshape the town
cards.text: The game features a new mechanic that makes the player the town mayor, allowing them to have more customization of their town than in previous games. While taking part in mayoral duties is not obligatory to play the game, being the head of town imparts two gameplay features new to the series: Public Works Projects and Ordinances. Public Works Projects allow players to collect funds from townsfolk and other visiting players to construct new objects such as bridges, fountains, and light poles, as well as add new facilities such as campsites and cafés. Ordinances gives players the ability to customize the way their town functions by passing laws, such as making the town wealthier, encouraging citizens to plant more flowers, or making the shops open earlier or later. Only the first person to register a save file on each copy of the game will be able to become mayor.

main.title: Paper Mario: Sticker Star
main.subtitle: Stickers give Paper Mario a new direction
main.summary: Paper Mario: Sticker Star is a 2012 role-playing video game developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 3DS.

cards.heading: Stickers give Paper Mario a new direction
cards.text: Paper Mario: Sticker Star is Intelligent Systems and Nintendo's 2012 role-playing adventure for Nintendo 3DS, the series' first handheld entry. Mario and Kersti travel across the Mushroom Kingdom to recover six Royal Stickers scattered by Bowser. Stickers collected in the world become single-use actions in battles or answers to puzzles, making the papercraft setting part of the rules. The design gives greater weight to those systems than to an elaborate story or large supporting party, distinguishing it from the earlier Paper Mario adventures.

cards.heading: Paperization turns objects into puzzle solutions
cards.text: A major facet of Sticker Star's gameplay is the use of collectible stickers, which are used to gain abilities to progress through the game. The player collects stickers that are found and peeled off from various areas in the environment. Additionally, the player can purchase stickers using coins or receive them from non-playable characters (NPC). The player has limited inventory space, with larger stickers taking up more room. Stickers are used both in combat and for interacting with the environment. The player can enter a state called "Paperization", which will lay the screen down flat to reveal additional secrets not visible regularly. Real-world objects can be found, known in-game as "Things", such as baseball bats and scissors, that can be turned into special types of stickers called "Thing Stickers", which are often needed to solve puzzles in the overworld. For example, a Fan Thing Sticker can be placed in strategic areas in the environment and, when activated, creates wind that moves or destroys obstacles.

cards.heading: Every attack spends a sticker
cards.text: As in previous games, combat in Sticker Star takes place in turn-based battles which are initiated when Mario comes into contact with enemies in the overworld. The player's available attacks are determined by the stickers on hand from their inventory. For example, possession of the Jump sticker can be used to attack an enemy by jumping on it. Certain kinds of attacks are required depending on the enemy being fought; an enemy wearing a spiked helmet cannot be jumped on and must instead be attacked using a different kind of sticker, like a hammer. Thing Stickers are used to inflict more damage on enemies, and certain types of Thing Stickers are required to make boss battles easier. Each sticker is removed from play after one use, making it necessary for the player to consistently collect new stickers. The player increases their maximum health points (HP) and other stats through collection of HP-Up hearts, which give Mario five more health points and stronger attacks.

cards.heading: A shorter episodic adventure changes the formula
cards.text: The team removed the earlier partner system because it conflicted with sticker-based play. Shigeru Miyamoto also asked for characters from the established Super Mario world and a reduced emphasis on story. Writer Taro Kudo developed an episodic structure around the world map and separate levels, allowing shorter sessions suited to the handheld.

main.title: Call of Duty: Black Ops II
main.subtitle: Two eras and a branching campaign from Treyarch
main.summary: Call of Duty: Black Ops II is a 2012 first-person shooter game developed by Treyarch and published by Activision.

cards.heading: Black Ops reaches two eras and new platforms
cards.text: Treyarch developed Call of Duty: Black Ops II, published by Activision in November 2012 for Windows, PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360, followed by Wii U. It continues Black Ops across two periods, with a branching campaign and a future setting. A separate PlayStation Vita game, Black Ops: Declassified, accompanied the release.

cards.heading: Two generations of Mason pursue Raul Menendez
cards.text: In the 1980s, the player switches control between Alex Mason and Frank Woods, the former being one of the protagonists from Black Ops, while in 2025, the player assumes control of Mason's son, David (codenamed "Section"). Both time periods involve the characters pursuing Raul Menendez, a Nicaraguan arms dealer and later terrorist, who is responsible for kidnapping David in the 80s and later sparking a Second Cold War in 2025. The campaign features non-linear gameplay and has multiple endings. Locations featured in the game include Angola, Myanmar, Afghanistan, Nicaragua, Pakistan, the Cayman Islands, Panama, Yemen, the United States, and Haiti.

cards.heading: Branching missions and futuristic warfare
cards.text: Development for the game began soon after the release of Black Ops, with Activision promising that the follow-up would bring "meaningful innovation" to the Call of Duty franchise. Black Ops II is the first game in the series to feature futuristic warfare technology and the first to present branching storylines driven by player choice as well as selecting weapons before starting story mode missions. It also offers a 3D display option. The game was officially revealed on May 1, 2012, following a set of leaked information released during the previous months.

cards.heading: A record launch, praised multiplayer and Zombies
cards.text: Black Ops II received mostly positive reviews from critics, with praise for its gameplay variety, story, multiplayer, Zombies mode, and villain, while its Strike Force missions received criticism. Retrospective reviewers consider it one of the best games in the series. The game was a commercial success; within 24 hours of its release, it grossed over $500 million. It had remained the largest entertainment launch of all time until the release of Grand Theft Auto V (2013). By November 2013, the game had sold over 24 million copies, making it one of the series' best-selling entries.

cards.heading: How later Black Ops games extend the story
cards.text: Sequels to the game continued or expanded the storyline: Call of Duty: Black Ops III (2015) acts as a direct sequel; Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War (2020) is set between the events of Black Ops and Black Ops II; Call of Duty: Black Ops 6 (2024) is set after Black Ops II's flashback missions; and Call of Duty: Black Ops 7 (2025) is set after the events of Black Ops II.

main.title: Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed
main.subtitle: SEGA’s worlds become transforming racetracks
main.summary: Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed is a kart racing game developed by Sumo Digital and published by Sega.

cards.heading: SEGA’s worlds become transforming racetracks
cards.text: Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed is a kart racing game developed by Sumo Digital and published by Sega. It was released for the PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, and Wii U in November 2012; for PlayStation Vita in December 2012; for Windows in January 2013; for Nintendo 3DS in February 2013; and for Android and iOS devices in January 2014. The PS3 and Wii U versions of the game were released in Japan on May 15, 2014.

cards.heading: Cars turn into boats and aircraft
cards.text: A blue transformation gate changes a vehicle from car to boat or plane as the race moves between road, water and air. Each form asks for a different reading of the course. Cars build boost through drifts and aerial tricks; boats react to waves that can also launch a stunt. Planes move vertically as well as sideways, with rolls and air-drifts providing ways to dodge and gain speed. Some tracks change between laps, so remembering the first circuit is not enough. More than twenty Sega characters share routes built around this shifting relationship between vehicle and terrain.

cards.heading: World Tour draws on SEGA’s history
cards.text: World Tour connects races through a branching series of challenges. Some ask for drifting, traffic avoidance or attacks on large tanks; completing them at different difficulties earns stars that open new routes, characters and modifications. Racing also gives each character experience, unlocking changes to vehicle statistics. Sixteen new tracks draw on Sega games including Panzer Dragoon, Golden Axe and Burning Rangers, alongside four returning locations and mirrored layouts. Online races and console split-screen let others share these courses. The Wii U version adds GamePad features and supports a fifth local player, changing how a group can join the race.

main.title: Wii U
main.subtitle: Two Screens, One Home Console
main.summary: Nintendo's first HD home console combines a television with a touchscreen GamePad, creating different views and roles for players in the same room.

cards.heading: Nintendo introduces Wii U
cards.text: Nintendo launched Wii U in North America on November 18, 2012, followed by Europe on November 30 and Japan on December 8. Its GamePad pairs a 6.2-inch touchscreen with the television, giving games a second view for maps, tools or a separate player role. Nintendo's first HD home console also includes Miiverse, Nintendo Network and compatibility with Wii software and accessories.

cards.heading: The GamePad's second screen
cards.text: The GamePad combines a touchscreen, sticks, buttons, motion sensors, camera and microphone. It can show an inventory or map while action continues on the television; supported games can also move play entirely to its display. The player must remain within range of the console, alternating attention between the personal and shared screens as a game requires.

cards.heading: Different roles in Nintendo Land
cards.text: Nintendo Land demonstrates asymmetric multiplayer. The GamePad holder may see information hidden from people using Wii Remotes and watching the television. Different views create distinct roles in a chase or cooperative task, giving the second screen a purpose beyond displaying more information.

cards.heading: Miiverse communities
cards.text: Miiverse gathered communities around games, with messages, stylus drawings and discussions accessible from the console. Some titles placed community comments or hints within play. The service let players encounter one another's contributions without being online together, continuing until its closure in 2017.

cards.heading: Keeping Wii games and controllers
cards.text: Wii discs and many peripherals, including Wii Remotes and Nunchuks, remain usable on Wii U. Transfer tools also preserve many earlier digital purchases. Multiplayer games can combine those controllers with the GamePad. The continuity helped existing owners reuse equipment, though the name and resemblance to Wii also made the new console harder to distinguish commercially.

main.title: New Super Mario Bros. U
main.subtitle: Mario joins the Wii U launch in high definition
main.summary: Mario reaches high-definition worlds as a Wii U launch title. New Super Mario Bros. U carries forward cooperative platforming while sending the group back to rescue Peach and her castle.

cards.heading: Cooperative Mario at the Wii U launch
cards.text: New Super Mario Bros. U is a 2012 platform game developed and published by Nintendo as a launch title for the Wii U. A sequel to New Super Mario Bros. Wii and the fourth and final entry in the New Super Mario Bros. series, following New Super Mario Bros. 2, it is the first Super Mario game to feature high-definition graphics. The plot follows Mario on his way to rescue Princess Peach and her castle from Bowser. The game retains the cooperative multiplayer mode from its prior entry.

cards.heading: Boost and Miiverse use the new console
cards.text: Development of New Super Mario Bros. U started after the release of New Super Mario Bros. Wii, and the game was revealed at E3 2011. Takashi Tezuka explained that he created the game to take advantage of the Wii U, introducing the Boost mode and Miiverse integration.

cards.heading: Reception, Luigi and the later Deluxe port
cards.text: The game received generally positive reviews from critics who praised its gameplay, graphics, and additions; but it was criticized for its unoriginality compared to prior titles and for having what some perceived as an uninteresting atmosphere. The game became the third best-selling Wii U game, and received an expansion pack named New Super Luigi U as part of the "Year of Luigi" campaign. A Nintendo Switch port named New Super Mario Bros. U Deluxe was released worldwide on January 11, 2019, followed by a release for China on December 10, 2019. As of March 2025, both versions combined have sold over 24 million copies.

main.title: ZombiU
main.subtitle: A survivor in a London overrun
main.summary: ZombiU is a first-person survival horror game developed by Ubisoft Montpellier and published by Ubisoft.

cards.heading: A survivor in a London overrun
cards.text: ZombiU is a first-person survival horror game developed by Ubisoft Montpellier and published by Ubisoft. It was released for the Wii U as a launch title in November 2012. In the game, the player assumes control of a human survivor amid a 2012 zombie apocalypse. Featuring a permadeath system, it uses the Wii U GamePad extensively to scan the environment and maintain the survivor's inventory. The game was released under the name Zombi for PlayStation 4, Windows, and Xbox One in August 2015. The port, handled by Straight Right, added new melee weapons and removed the multiplayer feature.

cards.heading: Death leaves equipment with the next threat
cards.text: Searching rooms and bodies yields ammunition, medicine and materials for barricades or weapon upgrades. Beds save progress, and routes can lead back to the safe house. Death is permanent for an individual survivor: the next character must confront the previous one as a zombie to recover their equipment. Shared online features could also place other players' dead characters and clues in the world.

cards.heading: The GamePad makes inventory management dangerous
cards.text: The game's controls make extensive use of the Wii U GamePad. During normal play, the touchscreen manages player inventory and displays a mini-map of the immediate area (indicating the locations of the player and nearby enemies). The touchscreen is also used for context-sensitive actions such as executions, escaping from enemies, and hacking combination locks. The GamePad's gyroscope, which allows the controller to sense its rotation and tilt in three-dimensional space, is also used. While viewing the touchscreen, a player can move the controller to scan different areas to find items. While performing these actions, the television's perspective switches to a fixed third-person view of the player character and the surrounding area. The player is vulnerable to attack in this state, and must watch the GamePad's touchscreen and the television screen in to avoid harm. The Wii U camera allows players to import a face, which will be "zombified", into the game.

cards.heading: A Rabbids project becomes survival horror
cards.text: Ubisoft was approached by Nintendo to develop a mature game for the Wii U. Originally envisioned as a spin-off of the Raving Rabbids franchise and a fast-paced first-person shooter, Killer Freaks from Outer Space (with small, agile monsters), the game was retooled as ZombiU after the development team realized that the Wii U GamePad was suitable for slower-paced games. Many of the game's features, including the GamePad functionality and the permadeath system, went through several iterations. Among other video games, ZombiU was influenced by Resident Evil, Condemned: Criminal Origins and Peter Jackson's King Kong. London was chosen as the game's setting because of its blend of modern and historic architecture and its rich history. Ubisoft Bucharest led development of the game's multiplayer portion.

main.title: Nintendo Land
main.subtitle: Nintendo’s worlds become a shared theme park
main.summary: Nintendo Land is a 2012 party video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Wii U.

cards.heading: Nintendo’s worlds become a shared theme park
cards.text: Nintendo Land is Nintendo's 2012 Wii U party game, built as a theme park with twelve attractions based on familiar series. Mario, Zelda and other characters provide settings for activities designed around the GamePad's touchscreen and motion controls. Some players use that controller while others hold Wii Remotes, giving people different information or tasks within the same game. Released with the console at launch, it introduced Wii U through shared play rather than a technical explanation. An Attraction Tour links the activities into a tournament, while individual attractions demonstrate different ways of sharing the screens.

cards.heading: One ghost sees what the other players cannot
cards.text: In Luigi's Ghost Mansion, one player controls an invisible ghost on the GamePad while up to four others search the house with flashlights. The television shows the rooms and trackers, but usually hides the ghost. A vibrating Wii Remote warns a tracker that it is close. Shining a flashlight on it reduces its health; the ghost instead tries to ambush everyone and make them faint. Other trackers can revive a fallen companion, but their lights need replacement batteries. The different screens turn a simple pursuit into a contest between what one person can see and what the group can infer.

cards.heading: An exhibition becomes Nintendo Land
cards.text: The team's goal was to create a product that showcased all the features the new console could do. This led to a problem, as unlike the similar Wii Sports, the games were not inherently related. Early on one staff member suggested that they attempt to do something that would unite the various Nintendo  franchises. As the team considered this too grand a concept, the idea was at first not taken seriously. The developers initially decided to present the theme as an "Expo" which lead to the theme park concept. Although most attractions were easy to theme, the team struggled with some: Metroid Blast was initially themed around Star Fox, while at one point it was considered to theme Donkey Kong Crash Course around either Excitebike or 1080° Snowboarding.

main.title: Hitman: Absolution
main.subtitle: Agent 47 becomes a protector
main.summary: Hitman: Absolution is a 2012 action stealth game developed by IO Interactive and published by Square Enix Europe.

cards.heading: Agent 47 becomes a protector
cards.text: IO Interactive's Hitman: Absolution follows Agent 47 as he protects a teenage girl whose enhanced abilities make her valuable to criminal groups and his former employers, the ICA. The campaign takes him through a succession of locations with different ways to reach an objective. Contracts adds custom targets and conditions that players could share using the existing missions.

cards.heading: Disguises and environments offer different approaches
cards.text: Agent 47 can approach a target through force, disguise or an apparently ordinary accident. A bottle or brick may distract someone; poisoned coffee, collapsing scaffolding or another environmental mechanism can turn observation into an attack. Disguises allow him to move among people rather than simply avoid them, while Instinct helps track enemies. Each chapter places these options within a particular location, from a mansion to a courthouse or hotel. Choosing a route means deciding which people and objects can make the objective possible without drawing attention.

cards.heading: The return of Agent 47 takes shape
cards.text: Plans for another Hitman emerged after 2007, with development confirmed in 2009 and the Absolution title revealed in 2011. William Mapother initially performed Agent 47, but David Bateson returned to provide the voice after fan objections. Mapother's motion-capture performance remained in the finished game.

main.title: PlayStation All-Stars Battle Royale
main.subtitle: PlayStation characters meet in Battle Royale
main.summary: PlayStation All-Stars Battle Royale is a 2012 crossover fighting game developed by SuperBot Entertainment and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Vita.

cards.heading: PlayStation characters meet in Battle Royale
cards.text:
PlayStation All-Stars Battle Royale is a 2012 crossover fighting game developed by SuperBot Entertainment and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Vita. It features various characters drawn from video game franchises owned by or strongly associated with PlayStation competing against each other in multiplayer battles.

Development of PlayStation All-Stars Battle Royale began in 2009 under the working title of Title Fight. The game's existence was leaked prior to its official announcement in April 2012, along with a significant number of its playable characters. PlayStation All-Stars Battle Royale was one of the first games to be included in Sony's cross-buy program, allowing those who purchased the game for PlayStation 3 to receive a free copy of the PlayStation Vita port.

cards.heading: Super Moves turn AP into knockouts
cards.text: Up to four characters fight on a two-dimensional stage, but ordinary attacks build power rather than directly deciding the result. Hitting opponents produces AP orbs, and throws can strip power from a rival. Filling the meter opens three levels of Super Moves, which defeat opponents and score points. A cheaper attack may cover only a short distance; saving for a stronger one can produce several eliminations before it expires. Characters from God of War, PaRappa the Rapper, Infamous and other series therefore share a contest about when to spend the power gathered during a fight.

cards.heading: Two worlds collide in every arena
cards.text: Battles take place in one of fifteen different battle arenas, with many featuring elements and stage hazards that can damage characters and cause them to lose AP. Each stage is based on a combination of two games, such as "Sandover Village" (based on Jak and Daxter and Hot Shots Golf), "Dreamscape" (based on LittleBigPlanet and Buzz!), "Stowaways" (based on Uncharted and BioShock Infinite), and "Hades" (based on God of War and Patapon). As time passes, a stage's second representation takes hold, usually introducing an additional hazard into the level. During gameplay, item pick-ups will spawn on the battlefield, such as the Hedgehog Grenade from Resistance, the Gravity Shield from Wipeout, Baumusu's Axe from Rise of the Kasai, and Razor Claws from Ratchet & Clank. These items can be used to augment a player or attack an opponent, causing them to lose AP. Both stage hazards and items can be disabled in the game's options menu.
